title: Direct view of exciton and carrier dynamics in twisted bilayer graphene
authors: Gianmarco Gatti, Anders S. Mortensen, Zhihao Jiang, Alfred J. H. Jones, Gesa-R. Siemann, Thomas S. Nielsen, Søren Ulstrup, Naina Kushwaha, Bruce Weaver, Yu Zhang, Emma Springate, Charlotte E. Sanders, Vibha Reddy, Ulrich Starke, Philip Hofmann
abstract: Twisted bilayer graphene (tBLG) on H-intercalated SiC (twist angle of $9 \pm 1^{\circ}$) is studied by position\mbox{-}, time\mbox{-}, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Both graphene layers are hole doped, with a Dirac-point offset of 30~meV. Time-resolved ARPES near the van Hove singularity reveals a spectral feature within the hybridization-induced band gap, together with excited electrons in the conduction band. The in-gap feature exhibits distinct dynamics, and its binding energy and $k$-space location are consistent with the proposed non-hydrogenic ``ghost-Fano'' exciton arising from destructive interference between two nearly degenerate excitonic channels. Near the Dirac points, the twist separates the largely layer-polarized Dirac cones in momentum space, providing direct layer selectivity. We find markedly different peak electronic temperatures in the two graphene layers, even though their subsequent cooling dynamics are very similar. We attribute this to an ultrafast interlayer redistribution of electronic energy, driven by an interlayer electric field that arises from the different doping in the layers.
summary: This work uses time-resolved ARPES to probe the dynamics of excitons and hot carriers in twisted bilayer graphene. The authors successfully identify a 'ghost-Fano' exciton signature and reveal that an inherent interlayer electric field causes the two graphene layers to reach different peak electronic temperatures. This demonstrates how electrostatic asymmetry can control non-equilibrium energy flow in correlated 2D systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the dynamics of excitons and charge carriers in twisted bilayer graphene (tBLG) to understand interlayer energy transfer and correlated electronic states.
main_result: The research identified a 'ghost-Fano' exciton signature and demonstrated that an interlayer electric field drives an ultrafast, asymmetric redistribution of electronic energy between the two graphene layers.
method: Time-resolved Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (TR-ARPES) was employed to track spectral features and measure time-dependent electronic temperatures.
model_or_system: The system is twisted bilayer graphene (tBLG) on SiC at a twist angle of $9 \pm 1^\circ$. The analysis involves modeling carrier cooling using a three-temperature model and interpreting spectral features via exciton theory.
key_observables: Spectral features in the hybridization-induced band gap (ghost-Fano exciton), layer-resolved electronic temperatures ($T_e$), and time-dependent photoemission intensity differences.
important_parameters: Twist angle ($9 \pm 1^\circ$), doping offset (30 meV), interlayer electric field ($\approx 0.1 	ext{ V/nm}$), and characteristic decay times ($	au_X = 300 	ext{ fs}$).
main_assumptions: The binding energy estimate from energy separation is approximate, and the temperature asymmetry analysis assumes energy transfer occurs during the initial excitation/thermalization stage.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate ARPES intensity maps, time-dependent photoemission intensity differences for exciton/conduction band features, and plots showing the distinct, asymmetric evolution of electronic temperature in the top versus bottom graphene layers.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from characterizing the tBLG structure and observing the exciton signature via ARPES, to quantifying the layer-dependent carrier cooling dynamics, and finally attributing the temperature asymmetry to interlayer energy transfer driven by doping-induced fields.
why_interesting: The study provides direct experimental evidence of non-equilibrium energy coupling and correlated excitonic physics in a tunable 2D material system, which is highly relevant for understanding correlated electronic states in novel quantum materials.
